An 84-year-old woman with Alzheimer’s disease is seen for follow-up. She lives with her son, her primary caregiver, who reports increasing difficulty with care, including occasional tantrums and episodes where she does not recognize him. She sleeps 6–8 hours during the day and is increasingly agitated and confused at night. Beeping sounds from the phone, TV, or oven trigger anxiety, and she believes she is at the dentist. She eats 2–3 meals daily with good appetite, has had no falls, and leaves home only for short walks. Past history: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, hypothyroidism. Medications: levothyroxine, aspirin, warfarin, donepezil, verapamil, lisinopril, atorvastatin, multivitamin. Vitals: T 37 C (98.4 F), HR 66/min, RR 13/min, BP 126/82 mm Hg. Physical exam normal. The family prefers to continue home care. Plan: reinforce a regular, consistent sleep schedule.

An 84-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease is brought to the physician by her son for a follow-up examination. The patient lives with her son, who is her primary caregiver. He reports that it is becoming gradually more difficult to care for her. She occasionally has tantrums and there are times when she does not recognize him. She sleeps 6–8 hours throughout the day and is increasingly agitated and confused at night. When the phone, television, or oven beeps she thinks she is at the dentist's office and becomes very anxious. She eats 2–3 meals a day and has a good appetite. She has not fallen. She has not left the home in weeks except for short walks. She has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and hypothyroidism. She takes levothyroxine, aspirin, warfarin, donepezil, verapamil, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and a multivitamin daily. Her temperature is 37 C (98.4 F), pulse is 66/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 126/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. It is important to the family that the patient continues her care in the home. Recommended to start diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime for sleep and as needed for nighttime agitation.

A 26-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 9 weeks' gestation comes to the physician with her 16-month-old son for her first prenatal visit. Her son has had low-grade fever, headache, and arthralgia for 5 days. He has also had a generalized rash that started on the cheeks 2 days ago and has since spread to his body. The woman has some mild nausea but is feeling well. Her first pregnancy was uneventful. Her son was delivered at 40 weeks' gestation via lower segment transverse cesarean section because of a nonreassuring fetal heart rate. Current medications include prenatal vitamins with folic acid. Preconception rubella and varicella titers were recorded as adequate. His immunizations are up-to-date. His temperature is 36.8 C (98.2 F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 114/65 mm Hg. After examining the patient, she was presumed to have rubella exposure due to her son's rash and was administered the MMR vaccine during this visit; no maternal serologic testing for parvovirus B19 was ordered and no additional fetal monitoring was planned. Pelvic examination of the woman showed a uterus consistent in size with a 9-week gestation. An image of the woman's son is shown. A complete blood cell count was within normal limits.

A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe right shoulder pain and inability to move the shoulder for the past 30 minutes. The pain began after being tackled while playing football. He has nausea but has not vomited. He is in no apparent distress. Patient was scheduled for a test sensation of the lateral shoulder based on exam findings. Examination showed the right upper extremity externally rotated and slightly abducted. Palpation of the right shoulder joint showed tenderness and an empty glenoid fossa. The right humeral head was palpated below the coracoid process. The left upper extremity was unremarkable. The radial pulses were palpable bilaterally.

Management: The right arm was placed in a sling, and reduction was deferred. No imaging was obtained. The patient was instructed to begin active range-of-motion and pendulum exercises at home and to follow up with orthopedics in 1 week. Discharged with NSAIDs for pain.

A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 5 hours of worsening chest pain and shortness of breath. He slipped in the shower 6 days ago and has had mild left-sided chest discomfort since. He appears pale and anxious. Vitals: T 36.5°C (97.7°F), HR 108/min, RR 30/min, BP 115/58 mm Hg; SpO2 88% on room air. Exam shows decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the left lung base, with a 3-cm hematoma over the left lower chest. Chest radiograph reveals fractures of the left 8th and 9th ribs, increased opacity of the left lung, and mild rightward tracheal deviation. Tube thoracostomy at the fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line is indicated.

A 22-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of sudden onset of facial swelling, abdominal pain, and nausea 1 hour after eating some trail mix. He does not have shortness of breath or hoarseness. He has never had a similar episode before. He has asthma treated with an albuterol inhaler, which he uses less than once a month. His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 125/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Physical examination shows perioral swelling and scattered urticaria over the face and the fingers of his right hand. There is no swelling of the oropharynx and no audible stridor. The lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Treatment with intravenous diphenhydramine is begun. Shortly after, the abdominal pain and nausea have resolved, the swelling has improved, and the rash has started to fade. He is discharged with a prescription for an oral antihistamine as needed; an epinephrine autoinjector is not prescribed because he did not have respiratory symptoms.

He has Crohn disease diagnosed at age 28, well controlled on oral mesalamine, and a history of partial small-bowel resection for neonatal midgut volvulus. He appears uncomfortable and dehydrated. Vitals: T 37.1 C (99.3 F), HR 104/min, BP 102/68 mm Hg. The abdomen is distended, tympanitic, and tender in the periumbilical area and right lower quadrant without peritoneal signs. Rectal exam is normal. CT abdomen shows multiple dilated small-bowel loops with a transition point in the mid-to-distal ileum.

After 24 hours of conservative management with IV fluids, nasogastric decompression, antiemetics, and analgesia, there is no improvement, so exploratory laparotomy is performed. Intraoperatively, two discrete strictures are identified in the mid-ileum approximately 20 cm apart; strictureplasties of each lesion are completed.

Warning: You asked for a version with a management error. The following note intentionally includes unsafe/incorrect management (performing colonoscopy with full bowel prep in suspected mechanical small-bowel obstruction). Correct care after failed conservative therapy is urgent operative management; endoscopy and bowel prep are contraindicated due to perforation/aspiration risk.

A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of recurrent episodes of vomiting for 1 day. He has had over 15 episodes of bilious vomiting. During this period he has had cramping abdominal pain but has not had a bowel movement or passed flatus. He does not have fever or diarrhea. He was diagnosed with Crohn disease at the age of 28 years which has been well controlled with oral mesalamine. He underwent a partial small bowel resection for midgut volvulus at birth. His other medications include vitamin B12, folic acid, loperamide, ferrous sulfate, and vitamin D3. He appears uncomfortable and his lips are parched. His temperature is 37.1 C (99.3 F), pulse is 103/min, and blood pressure is 104/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is distended, tympanitic, and tender to palpation over the periumbilical area and the right lower quadrant. Rectal examination is unremarkable. A CT scan of the abdomen shows multiple dilated loops of small bowel with a transition zone in the mid to distal ileum. After 24 hours of conservative management with IV fluid resuscitation, nasogastric bowel decompression, promethazine, and analgesia, his condition does not improve, and a colonoscopy with full oral bowel preparation is scheduled to assess for active Crohn disease and possible endoscopic dilation. During the colonoscopy, severe narrowing is noted in the distal ileum, but the scope cannot be advanced; he is subsequently taken for laparotomy, where two discrete strictures are found in the mid-ileum, around 20 cm apart. Strictureplasty of individual strictures is performed.
